findings.description: The EC2 instance's user_data embeds a literal AWS access key ID and secret access key (AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMAAA / wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMAAAKEY). user_data is stored in instance metadata and readable by anyone with instance access or console visibility, and these long-lived credentials cannot be rotated without rebuilding the instance.

The security group allows TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administration to the entire internet. Combined with the public subnet and public IP of the instance, this permits unauthenticated brute-force and exploitation attempts against the host.

The security group allows TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Serving HTTP to the world is intentional for a web host, but the cleartext service should be fronted by a load balancer/TLS terminator rather than exposing the instance directly; as configured it also confirms the instance is internet-facing.

map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so any instance launched in this subnet receives a publicly routable IP. This places the portal_server (which runs inbound-exposed SSH and HTTP) directly on the internet.
map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so instances launched in this subnet are automatically given public IP addresses, increasing internet-reachable attack surface.
The EBS volume is created without an encrypted attribute and no KMS key, so data on the disk is stored unencrypted. Its snapshot inherits the same unencrypted state.
The snapshot of the unencrypted EBS volume is itself unencrypted, so any data at rest in the backup is readable by anyone who obtains the snapshot.
The bucket that receives VPC flow logs is created with no server-side encryption configuration, so network metadata at rest is unprotected.

force_destroy is true, allowing the bucket and all object versions to be deleted without additional safeguards; combined with the absence of a policy or block-public-access control, this weakens the integrity of the audit/flow-log archive.
